history.title: Order Exception Cost Ledger Flatlay

style_when: the story is regulatory or contractual — a filing, a mandate, a rate notice, a certificate, a purchase order that changed the economics
prompt: Document still life, overhead flat-lay photograph of heavy matte paper documents on a textured dark wood desk surface. Top-down 90-degree view, 50mm lens with shallow depth of field. Even diffused daylight casting soft shadows. An annotated time-and-wage ledger showing deliberate physical handling sits off-centre, partially covering a discarded, muted vendor invoice. The paper tones are subtle, muted off-whites and greys. Asymmetric framing with generous editorial negative space. No legible text.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random letters, numbers, UI, watermarks, signatures
rationale: The story revolves around a financial calculation, a specific cost breakdown, and the contrast between a vendor's claimed invoice and internal wage reality. A document flatlay perfectly captures the forensic accounting and analytical nature of this revelation.
subject: an annotated time-and-wage ledger and a discarded vendor invoice
core_thesis: The true cost of an order exception is driven by the internal handle time and wage of the service rep, not an arbitrary flat fee quoted by a vendor.
core_conflict: Arbitrary vendor flat-fee claims vs the actual internal labor cost dictated by handle time and wages.
composition: asymmetric top-down 90-degree framing with the main ledger off-centre
alt_text: The $30 Exception Myth. An annotated time-and-wage ledger lying on top of a vendor invoice on a dark wooden desk.
caption: The $30 Exception Myth: How bad vendor math masks the real cost of broken orders.
title: The $30 Exception Myth
